title: Therapeutic Hypothermia for Neonatal Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy: Clinical Report
authors: AAP Committee on Fetus and Newborn
summary:
This AAP report updates the 2014 guidance and reinforces cooling eligible newborns born at ≥36 weeks with moderate-to-severe HIE: start within 6 hours, target 33.5°C and continue 72 hours.

It clarifies selected younger or later-presenting infants and emphasizes rapid recognition, cooling-center consultation and coordinated transfer. Cooling is not established treatment for mild HIE; avoid hyperthermia even when therapeutic hypothermia is unsuitable.
findings: At 35 0/7–35 6/7 weeks, treatment may be considered after family discussion; below 35 weeks it is not recommended.
At 6–24 hours, selected moderate-to-severe HIE cases may be considered after discussing potentially small benefits and risks.
Transport cooling requires strict protocols; specialist evaluation should proceed urgently rather than awaiting transfer.

Eligibility: obtain cord or first-hour blood gas. NICHD criteria use pH ≤7.00 or base deficit ≥16 mmol/L; absent gas, pH 7.01–7.15 or deficit 10–15.9 additionally require an acute perinatal event and ventilation continuing 10 minutes or 10-minute Apgar ≤5. Moderate/severe encephalopathy or seizures is also required; modified Sarnat assessment uses ≥3 moderate/severe domains among consciousness, activity, posture, tone, primitive reflexes and autonomic function. Discuss borderline findings with the cooling center.

Safety: bradycardia, QT prolongation and thrombocytopenia occur. Deeper/prolonged cooling is not an improvement. Servo-controlled transport cooling reduces overcooling; passive cooling requires close core-temperature and vital-sign monitoring.

Continuous EEG is preferred; aEEG is an alternative when unavailable. MRI before discharge and developmental follow-up are part of specialist care. Cooling alters drug clearance; use neonatal pharmacy support.

Underlying preterm RCT (168 infants, 33–35 weeks): death/disability occurred in 29/83 cooled versus 20/69 normothermic infants; adjusted RR 1.11 (95% credible interval 0.74–2.00). Death occurred in 18/88 versus 9/78; adjusted RR 1.38 (0.79–2.85). These uncertain estimates do not establish safety or benefit for routine preterm cooling.

Underlying late-initiation RCT (168 infants ≥36 weeks): death/disability was 19/78 versus 22/79; adjusted posterior RR 0.86 (95% credible interval 0.58–1.29). Its 76% probability of any benefit is not definitive efficacy. The studied late-cooling course lasted 96 hours, unlike the standard early 72-hour regimen.

Mild-HIE COMET pilot (101 infants) did not improve cerebral MR biomarkers; baseline imbalance and a surrogate endpoint limit interpretation. It does not establish developmental benefit or equivalence.
comparator: Clinical-report recommendations; no new randomized comparison.
population: Newborns with suspected moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
shortTitle: AAP neonatal HIE: early recognition and cooling-center transfer
limitations: This clinical report is not a new trial. Preterm, delayed-initiation and mild-HIE evidence remains uncertain; their populations and regimens differ. Main-text/tables were reviewed, but embedded algorithm artwork and every cited paper were not independently inspected. Use the receiving center’s protocol.
intervention: Specialist-directed therapeutic hypothermia and coordinated transfer.
whyItMatters: An ED encountering a newborn with suspected HIE should urgently contact a cooling center. Presentation beyond 6 hours should prompt specialist assessment rather than automatic dismissal of possible eligibility.

primaryEndpoint: Prevention of death or moderate-to-severe neurodevelopmental impairment.
guidelineStrength: AAP key action statements; no formal GRADE categories assigned here. Conditional consideration must not become routine treatment.
